params.question: In the clinical vignette, a boy has serpiginous grey lines between his fingers and nocturnal pruritus, and several household members have begun scratching. Which feature is the strongest epidemiological clue pointing specifically to scabies?

answers.text: Presence of excoriated papules on the wrists and waistline

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Excoriated papules on the wrists and waistline are morphological findings suggestive of scabies, but they are not epidemiological clues. The epidemiological hallmark is the pattern of person-to-person transmission through close contacts.

answers.text: Worsening of the rash after topical corticosteroid use

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Steroid worsening occurs because immunosuppression permits mite proliferation, but this is a treatment response, not an epidemiological clue. Other conditions such as tinea incognito also worsen with steroids.

answers.text: Household clustering of pruritus with nocturnal predominance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Scabies spreads by prolonged skin-to-skin contact, causing household clustering. The nocturnal itch — driven by increased mite activity and bed warmth — combined with multiple affected contacts is the classic epidemiological signature of scabies.
Genital nodules are a highly suggestive morphological sign of scabies in males, but they represent a clinical finding on examination, not an epidemiological pattern of disease spread.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the vignette: the narration emphasises that the clue is 'not just the rash but the family clustering and the nocturnal itch.' Epidemiological clues describe disease transmission patterns, not individual lesion morphology.
Exactly right. The combination of household clustering and nocturnal itch is the epidemiological hallmark that should prompt a clinical diagnosis of scabies, even before examining for burrows.

params.question: In a patient with widespread pruritus, the absence of visible burrows reliably excludes a diagnosis of scabies.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Burrows are often destroyed by excoriation, so their absence does NOT exclude scabies. As the narration explains, 'much of the diagnosis comes from the company the lesions keep' — the characteristic distribution and contact history matter more than any single lesion.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Burrows are the pathognomonic lesion but are frequently obscured by scratching and excoriation. The diagnosis rests on the overall distribution pattern (web spaces, wrists, waistline, genitalia) and household contact clustering, not on finding a single lesion type.

interactions.label: Which combination of clinical features most reliably distinguishes atopic dermat

params.question: Which combination of clinical features most reliably distinguishes atopic dermatitis from scabies in a patient presenting with intense generalised pruritus?

answers.text: Flexural distribution in antecubital and popliteal fossae, sparing of web spaces and genitalia, and no household contact clustering

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Atopic dermatitis favours the antecubital and popliteal fossae, characteristically spares the finger web spaces and genitalia, lacks burrows, and does not produce household clustering — all features that reliably distinguish it from scabies.

answers.text: Severe nocturnal pruritus with excoriated papules on the trunk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Nocturnal pruritus with trunk excoriations occurs in both scabies and atopic dermatitis. These features alone are insufficient to distinguish the two conditions.

answers.text: Grouped itchy papules on exposed areas of the limbs without burrows

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Grouped papules on exposed sites suggest papular urticaria or insect bites, not atopic dermatitis. Atopic dermatitis has a flexural predilection, while insect bites favour exposed, uncovered skin.

Lichenification and post-inflammatory pigmentation occur in any chronic pruritic condition, including scabies. These non-specific secondary changes do not reliably distinguish atopic dermatitis from scabies.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the differential: atopic dermatitis favours antecubital and popliteal fossae, spares web spaces and genitalia, has no burrows, and shows no household clustering — these features together separate it from scabies.
Well analysed. The distinguishing triad is site distribution (flexural fossae versus web spaces and genitalia), absence of burrows, and lack of household clustering.

interactions.label: A 7-year-old girl with pediculosis capitis has not responded to two courses of p

params.question: A 7-year-old girl with pediculosis capitis has not responded to two courses of permethrin 1% lotion. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.text: Apply permethrin 5% cream to the scalp overnight

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Permethrin 5% cream is the scabicide formulation used for body application in scabies. For resistant head lice, the appropriate step is to switch to a different pediculicide class, not to increase the permethrin concentration.

answers.text: Hot-wash all clothing and bedding as the primary intervention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hot-washing clothing and bedding is the primary treatment for pediculosis corporis, where lice inhabit clothing seams. In pediculosis capitis, the lice live on the scalp and require topical pediculicide treatment; laundering is an adjunct, not the primary step.

answers.text: Begin oral ivermectin 200 micrograms per kilogram immediately

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oral ivermectin is reserved for resistant or extensive cases of pediculosis. The stepwise approach requires trying malathion 0.5% as second-line before escalating to systemic therapy, which carries additional adverse effect considerations.

answers.text: Prescribe malathion 0.5% lotion as the second-line pediculicide

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Malathion 0.5% lotion is the principal second-line agent for pediculosis capitis when permethrin resistance is suspected. It acts via a different mechanism and should be repeated after 7–10 days to target newly hatched nymphs.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the management algorithm: permethrin 1% is first-line for pediculosis capitis, malathion 0.5% lotion is the second-line agent for resistant cases, and oral ivermectin is reserved for extensive or truly refractory infestations.
Correct. The treatment ladder for resistant pediculosis capitis moves from permethrin 1% to malathion 0.5% before considering ivermectin for truly refractory cases.
